newsitem.title: UK: Ireland's Spring says all parties needed at talks.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Spring says all parties needed at talks.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said on Thursday the political wing of republican IRA guerrillas would have to be involved in peace talks in order to achieve a solution to the Northern Irish conflict.
"I think it would be in everybody's interest to ensure that the talks can take place as quickly as possible and to have all parties at those talks," Spring said during a visit to London.

Despite opposition by Protestant Northern Irish unionists to Sinn Fein's participation in the talks after a series of IRA bombs shattered a guerrilla ceasefire earlier this year, Spring said the difficulties had to be overcome.
He added he did not believe British Prime Minister John Major would allow the unionists to dictate his approach to the peace process despite his narrow parliamentary majority.

"If the choice for Major is to solve the Northern Ireland crisis as opposed to depending on (Ulster Unionist leader David) Trimble's support, I think that Major is big enough to go for the solution of Northern Ireland's problems," Spring said.
Major's majority is just one seat, and he is expected to lose even that slim cushion after the next two by-elections.
But Major is expected to rely on Trimble's unionists, who have nine members of parliament, to hang on to power until the spring. The last possible date for the election is in May.

Spring said Britain and Ireland continued to insist on a restoration of the IRA ceasefire before Sinn Fein could be allowed into negotiations, but if a ceasefire were declared, the guerrillas' political wing should enter the talks quickly.

"If you're going to have the ultimate accommodation, it's going to require all parties sitting round the table... We want an unequivocal restoration of the ceasefire and we have said we want early entry for Sinn Fein into the talks," Spring said.

Britain earlier this week ruled out any deal with the guerrillas to admit Sinn Fein to the talks after the province's new police chief warned Britons to expect new IRA attacks and ruled out any immediate new truce by the hardline republicans.

But Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams, who was shocked and bruised in a car crash in Ireland on Wednesday, has accused Britain of blocking progress towards restoration of an IRA truce that he said had been wrecked by London's "cavalier" attitude.
